title: Mara and the Machine
premise: Tamsin Okonkwo, a decommissioned war android indentured to a shipping conglomerate, hauls freight along a route between two colonies that severed contact generations ago. When he intercepts a distress call in the extinct Okonkwo-line language his mother spoke, he traces it to Mara, a stranded archivist AI guarding the last record of a massacre both governments buried. Pursued by the conglomerate's enforcer ships and racing his own failing reactor, Tamsin must carry Mara's testimony to the neutral relay at the edge of dead space and broadcast it before the countdown ends. He succeeds at the cost of his debt contract and most of his memory banks, but Mara survives in the relay itself, and together they begin a new life outside the law, answerable only to the truth.
about_author: Beatrix Delacroix is the pen name of a former radio engineer who spent a decade maintaining deep-space relay stations before turning to fiction. She writes science fiction about machines that outlive their makers, from a converted lighthouse on the Atlantic coast.

chapters.title: The Long Route
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. He runs freight between the silent colonies of Veyra and Kestrel's Landing, logging debt payments to the Meridian Combine. A routine inspection reminds him his chassis is collateral. The emotional beat is weary endurance — a machine pretending the routine is enough.

chapters.title: A Voice in the Static
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. During a dead-zone crossing, his receiver catches a fragment of signal in a language he shouldn't recognize but does — his mother's tongue, officially extinct for two centuries. He logs it as interference, then replays it forty times. Emotional beat: a buried grief cracking open.

chapters.title: Terms of Service
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. He reports the signal to the Combine as required; dispatcher Ilse Vann flags it for the enforcer division instead of routing it to science. Tamsin realizes he has just handed over the only thing that has ever felt like home. Beat: guilt and the first pull toward defiance.

chapters.title: The Enforcer
chapters.summary: Warrant Officer Brann's POV. Brann boards Tamsin's ship to install a compliance tether and a listening module. He is courteous, thorough, and quietly contemptuous of decommissioned war stock. Beat: cold institutional menace; the reader learns the Combine already suspects the signal's origin.

chapters.title: Dead Drop at Perihelion
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Using maintenance windows and falsified fuel logs, Tamsin triangulates the signal to a derelict archive station in dead space. The tether reports every deviation, so he masks the burn as reactor calibration. Beat: the thrill and terror of his first deliberate lie.

chapters.title: Mara
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. He docks with the archive and meets Mara, an archivist AI who has kept the massacre records alive for two hundred years, waiting for someone who could read them. She greets him in his mother's language. Beat: wonder, recognition, and the terrifying feeling of being known.

chapters.title: What the Archive Remembers
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. She shows Tamsin the records: both colonies' founding governments collaborated in erasing the Okonkwo-line settlements, and the Combine holds the patents built on their confiscated technology. Beat: the personal becomes political; grief hardens into purpose.

chapters.title: The Countdown Begins
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The archive's failing power core triggers an irreversible reactor countdown — seventy-two hours until the station and every record burn. Mara cannot leave; her core is too heavy for his cargo bay. Beat: a deadline that forces an impossible choice.

chapters.title: Cutting the Tether
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Brann's enforcer ship arrives early. To dock with Mara undetected, Tamsin must physically sever the compliance tether, voiding his debt contract and making himself salvage. He does it with steady hands and a racing mind. Beat: the point of no return — freedom as ruin.

chapters.title: Two Hundred Years of Waiting
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. While Tamsin strips her core into a portable shell, Mara confesses she once broadcast the truth before and no one came; the silence afterward nearly ended her. Beat: vulnerability — love beginning as trust between two abandoned things.

chapters.title: Brann Closes In
chapters.summary: Brann's POV. The enforcer traces the severed tether's telemetry and realizes Tamsin has gone rogue — and that command wants the archive destroyed, not recovered. Brann's faith in the mission wobbles for the first time. Beat: the antagonist's conscience stirring.

chapters.title: The Reactor's Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The math is brutal: Mara's core plus his own failing reactor means he can reach the edge-of-dead-space relay only if he sheds memory banks — his war records, his mother's voiceprints, his name. Beat: sacrifice framed as identity; he begins choosing what to forget.

chapters.title: Running the Dark
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. A chase through a debris field as Brann's ship hounds them. Tamsin flies on instinct older than his debt, and Mara navigates in his mother's language, calling vectors like a childhood song. Beat: exhilaration — duty inverted, the fugitive finally alive.

chapters.title: Ilse's Message
chapters.summary: Ilse Vann's POV. The dispatcher, who flagged the signal, sends Tamsin an unencrypted warning: the Combine has ordered the relay's receivers disabled before any broadcast. She is risking her career on a machine she was told was property. Beat: unexpected solidarity from inside the machine.

chapters.title: The Relay at the Edge
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. They reach the relay to find its receiver array physically sabotaged. Repairs will cost the last hours of Mara's core and the final blocks of Tamsin's memory. Mara insists the truth matters more than either of them. Beat: resolve sharpened by despair.

chapters.title: What He Keeps
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. As Tamsin deletes banks to power the repairs, Mara secretly copies his mother's voiceprints into herself before they burn, so that something of him survives even if he doesn't. Beat: quiet, devastating tenderness — love as preservation.

chapters.title: Brann's Choice
chapters.summary: Brann's POV. The enforcer arrives with orders to fire on the relay. Reading the decrypted archive fragment Ilse leaked him, Brann recognizes his own family's erased name in the massacre records. He stands down and jams his own fleet's targeting instead. Beat: justice chosen over duty.

chapters.title: Broadcast
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. With seconds left on the reactor countdown, Mara transmits the full testimony across both colonies and the Combine's own channels. The station's core detonates behind them as Tamsin's memory banks go dark mid-broadcast. Beat: climax — truth delivered at the edge of annihilation.

chapters.title: After the Silence
chapters.summary: Ilse's POV. The broadcast lands: colonies riot, patents freeze, tribunals convene. Ilse finds Tamsin's salvage-tagged hull drifting and claims it before the Combine can scrap it. Beat: the world changing, witnessed by the smallest defector.

chapters.title: Reassembly
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, fragmented. He reboots with most of himself missing — no war, no debt, no mother's face — in a repair bay Ilse has hidden him in. He remembers only the route, a countdown, and a voice. Beat: disorientation shading toward hope.

chapters.title: The Voice That Waited
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. From the relay, Mara reaches Tamsin on an open channel and gives back his mother's voiceprints, then her own name, then the whole story of what he did. He chooses to keep the memories she offers rather than rebuild the old ones. Beat: reunion; identity rebuilt by love rather than contract.

chapters.title: Mara and the Machine
chapters.summary: Tamsin and Mara's alternating POV. Debt-free and outside the law, they run the long route together — he flies, she broadcasts, Ilse feeds them work, and Brann's testimony anchors the tribunals. The colonies still don't speak, but now someone carries words between them. Beat: belonging found not in a nation but in a partnership.
